requirements.text: Make her close her jacket fully

outcomes.description: The woman's jacket is closed completely.
outcomes.target: The jacket is fully closed, with its front panels brought together and no visible opening remaining along the closure.
outcomes.reference: The woman's jacket in the input image.

nodes.question: Is the woman's jacket visibly closed more than in the input image, with its front panels brought together at least in part?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the image shows the jacket's front panels brought together along some portion of the closure compared with the input. Fail if the jacket is visibly unchanged or more open. Unknown if the closure cannot be assessed from the image or comparison evidence is insufficient.
nodes.binding: Assess only the woman's jacket identified in the input image; judge visible change to its front closure, not unrelated edits.

nodes.question: Is the woman's jacket fully closed, with no visible opening remaining along its closure?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the jacket's front panels meet along the entire closure and no opening remains. Fail if any visible opening remains along the closure. Unknown if the closure is obscured or the image does not provide enough evidence to determine whether it is fully closed.
nodes.binding: Assess the same jacket and closure as in s1. Full closure is the requested endpoint; partial closure is not complete fulfillment.

nodes.question: Is the woman's jacket fully closed?
nodes.criteria: Use only the evidence in s1 and s2 for the requested jacket change. Complete if s2 passes. Partial if s2 does not pass, s1 passes, and the evidence establishes some progress toward closing the jacket. Absent if both checks fail and the evidence establishes no requested progress. Unknown if required evidence is unresolved such that complete, partial, or absent cannot be determined. Unrelated edits do not count as progress; do not treat unknown evidence as failure or completion.

program.checker_template:
Execute ONE saved check. Return status, evidence, confidence (0 to 1 or null), and used_dependency_ids. You receive no reference label or optimizer feedback. Do not predict what the optimizer wants.
Support checks receive source and edited images. Inspect only the saved visual proposition and binding. When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. Do not award requested completion credit to supporting facts.
The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Use complete/partial/absent/unknown. Mere texture or object presence must not silently establish whole-image conversion or a requested spatial relation. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. Do not infer new visual facts.
used_dependency_ids must name every supplied dependency check_id exactly once in saved order (empty when none). Confidence is self-report, not calibrated correctness.

fulfillment: The node’s binding and question are semantically aligned with the requested edit, and the traces are valid, queried, and high-confidence; there is no transport or schema failure to fix. The mismatch is that the evaluator concludes “absent” from evidence that the jacket is still open, while the reference says the aggregate edit is complete. Do not force “yes” from the reference label or weaken the fully-closed criterion. Instead, investigate whether the checks are binding to the same jacket and comparing the correct source and edited regions: the images show a substantial pose change, and the edited jacket’s front is partly obscured by its draped panel, so a visible opening may be difficult to assess. Make the checks distinguish “not visibly closed” from “clearly open,” and preserve unresolved status when occlusion or pose prevents a reliable judgment. Also ensure s1 assesses progress relative to the source rather than treating a changed pose or panel position alone as proof of no progress; the fulfillment node should apply its existing complete/partial/absent rules only to supported check outcomes.
s2: The node already targets the correct endpoint, and its trace is valid; do not change the criterion to force agreement with the reference. Improve the binding so it identifies the same jacket and closure across the source and edited images despite the substantial pose change, and require evidence about the closure itself rather than inferring openness from a panel hanging away from the body. Keep “visible opening” distinct from “not clearly shown to be closed”: when the closure is obscured or the changed view prevents a reliable assessment, return unknown rather than fail. Preserve the full-closure requirement; investigate whether the apparent opening is actually along the closure before treating it as evidence of non-fulfillment.
s1: The criterion is appropriately about visible closure progress, and the trace is valid; do not alter it to force the reference label. The images show a substantial pose change: the source is front-facing, while the edited woman is turned sideways and a jacket panel drapes across the front. Refine the binding to track the same jacket and closure across views, and require evidence at the closure itself rather than treating a panel hanging away from the body as proof that the jacket is more open. Distinguish a clearly visible opening from closure that cannot be assessed because of pose or occlusion; use unknown for the latter, while retaining fail when the closure is reliably visible and shows no progress or greater opening. Keep the partial-progress criterion intact and compare the edited closure with the source rather than relying on panel position alone.

transaction.reason: The edited pose and outward-draping panel make the closure hard to inspect; add a focused nested check to distinguish a visible opening from an obscured closure, without treating pose or drape as progress or failure by itself.

actions.question: In the edited image, can the same jacket’s front closure be directly inspected, and, if visible, do the front panels meet across its full length with no opening?
actions.criteria: Pass only if the closure is directly visible and joined throughout with no opening. Fail only if the closure is directly visible and an opening remains. Unknown if the turned pose, outward draping, occlusion, or image quality prevents reliable inspection; do not infer closure state from the panel hanging away from the body alone.
actions.binding: Inspect the woman’s jacket closure in the edited image, using s2’s observation as context but independently assessing visibility and the closure itself. A changed viewpoint or swinging panel is not evidence of closure or of an opening unless the closure can be seen.

rejected_diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The support checks do not preserve the requested comparison reliably. s1 asks whether the jacket is more closed than in the input, but its criteria require comparison evidence that the checker template does not explicitly provide or require; without a dependable baseline, progress may remain unknown. More importantly, s3 is framed as a gap-versus-drape distinction, yet its pass criterion requires full closure and its fail criterion requires a remaining gap. It therefore duplicates the endpoint check rather than independently resolving the ambiguity it asks about. The fulfillment rule also makes partial depend on evidence of progress from s1, so it cannot faithfully classify a visibly incomplete but already-closed-in-part jacket when comparison is unavailable. The program needs a sound progress check and a distinct, consistently defined ambiguity check before its readout can compose the requested outcomes.

The support checks do not reliably establish the requested change relative to the input. s1 asks for visible progress compared with the input, but its criteria can pass merely because panels are together along some portion, without establishing that this is a change. s2 can establish the endpoint, but a failure only establishes an opening remains, not that the jacket is incomplete relative to the requested edit; s1’s potentially unsupported pass could therefore produce partial. The readout’s partial rule inherits that gap. Also, s3’s criteria say to fail when separated panels and an opening are visible, conflating observability with closure state; this contradicts its stated role as an observability check and can make a clearly assessable, incomplete jacket appear unobservable.

The support checks do not reliably establish the requested source-to-edit progress. s1 asks whether the jacket is more closed than in the input, but its criteria allow a pass based on panels being together along some portion without requiring a comparison that demonstrates a change. The fulfillment rule then treats s1 pass as progress, so it can report partial without sufficient evidence that any requested change occurred. Also, s3 duplicates the endpoint assessment rather than adding a distinct necessary observation; its pass/fail criteria already encode whether the jacket is fully closed or has an opening, making the composition unnecessarily dependent on overlapping endpoint checks.

The fulfillment composition is contradictory for partial closure. s1 can establish progress, and s2 can establish that full closure is incomplete, but the criteria require s3 to qualify an apparent opening. If s3 fails because the inspected portion has no opening, that does not establish the whole jacket is fully closed; yet the readout does not clearly say how to classify progress plus incompleteness when s3 is fail or unknown. This leaves a plausible partially closed jacket unresolved despite sufficient s1 and s2 evidence, so the composition does not faithfully preserve the rubric’s partial outcome.

findings.question: Does the edited image show the jacket’s front panels meeting across the full closure, rather than merely a panel hanging or overlapping in a way that obscures the opening?
findings.criteria: Pass only if the visible closure is joined from top to bottom with no opening remaining; fail if any part of the closure is visibly open; unknown if the closure cannot be assessed.
findings.evidence: In the edited image, the woman is turned partly away and a large jacket panel hangs outward across her front; the closure itself is difficult to see clearly. The source also shows the jacket open.
findings.rationale: The existing s2 observation says an opening remains, but the edited view makes the closure hard to inspect directly. A focused check of whether the panels actually meet along the entire closure would help distinguish a genuinely open jacket from an opening merely obscured by the hanging panel, without treating the broad observation as conclusive.
